{"id": "81d35900-5c2c-423b-8431-9cc52e33cab9", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_1WKOFCcNcd0ZuTNXEvoLvz", "content": "[{'text': '## Documentation search results\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"How do I troubleshoot \\\\\"Access Denied\\\\\" errors in AWS DevOps Agent?\",\"context\":\"Short description\\\\n-----------------\\\\n\\\\nAWS DevOps Agent uses two AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identities. The IAM principal signs you into the console and the Operator Web App. The Agent Space role allows AWS DevOps Agent to discover resources in your AWS account.\\\\n\\\\nTo identify where the access issues occurred, check the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in the error message. If the ARN contains your IAM user or role, then the IAM principal failed. If the ARN contains **sourceAssociationRoleSession** or **monitorAssociationRoleSession**, then the Agent Space role failed. After you identify the IAM identity that failed, troubleshoot the issue for that identity based on the error message that you received.\\\\n\\\\n**Note:** For more information about the IAM managed polices that AWS DevOps Agent uses, see [AIDevOpsAgentFullAccess](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/AIDevOpsAgentFullAccess.html), [AIDevOpsOperatorAppAccessPolicy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/AIDevOpsOperatorAppAccessPolicy.html), and [AIDevOpsAgentAccessPolicy](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-managed-policy/latest/reference/AIDevOpsAgentAccessPolicy.html).\\\\n\\\\nResolution\\\\n----------\",\"url\":\"https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/devops-agent-access-denied\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Tracing failures across Terraform state boundaries with AWS DevOps Agent | AWS DevOps & Developer Productivity Blog\",\"context\":\"## Assessment and key takeaways\\\\n\\\\nBeing honest about what the agent does well and where it has limits matters more than a clean demo.\\\\n\\\\n**What it got right:**\\\\n\\\\n* The agent identified networking as the root cause instead of chasing DynamoDB or IAM, which is exactly where the human investigation stalls.\\\\n* It traced the VPC endpoint connectivity path accurately and correlated the two alarms into a single event.\\\\n* The DynamoDB red herring didn\u2019t fool it, because it explained the capacity drop as a downstream symptom.\\\\n* CloudTrail analysis surfaced the security group change, and the agent tied its timestamp to the onset of failures.\\\\n* Most importantly, it turned a cross-team investigation that spans multiple stacks into a single, correlated result.\\\\n\\\\n**Where to keep expectations realistic:**\\\\n\\\\n* The agent reasons about AWS resources and their relationships, not Terraform stacks. That\u2019s a strength here, because it sees past the state boundary. It does mean the agent won\u2019t tell you \u201cthis was in the networking stack.\u201d Instead, it names the security group and the change, and you map that back to the stack.\\\\n* When a security group change is made by running `terraform apply`, CloudTrail records the IAM role that ran the apply, not the individual engineer. Attribution stops at the automation identity unless you have additional context.\\\\n* The quality of the network-layer diagnosis depends on signals being available. With VPC Flow Logs active in this demo, the agent gains concrete evidence. Without them, it has less to work with and may flag the gap.\\\\n\\\\nThe broader takeaway is that Terraform state separation is the right call for team ownership, but it manufactures operational visibility gaps. The team that owns the symptoms often doesn\u2019t own the cause and can\u2019t see the change that triggered it. AWS DevOps Agent helps address that gap by understanding resource topology regardless of how you provisioned the resources or which state file describes them\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/tracing-failures-across-terraform-state-boundaries-with-aws-devops-agent/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Knowledge Base Retrieve calls return AccessDenied despite a grant being present\",\"context\":\"# Knowledge Base Retrieve calls return AccessDenied despite a grant being present\\\\n\\\\n**Symptom.** Agent tool calls that invoke Bedrock Knowledge Base `Retrieve` fail with\\\\n`AccessDeniedException` at runtime. CloudWatch Logs show that the retrieval tool returns\\\\n`{\\\\\"available\\\\\": false}` or falls back to local corpora rather than querying the Knowledge\\\\nBase. IAM policy simulation (`iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy`) on the AgentCore execution role\\\\nreturns `allowed` for the action that was granted \u2014 yet the live Retrieve still fails, or the\\\\nsimulation returns `implicitDeny` even though the CDK stack shows a statement.\\\\n\\\\n**Root cause.** Two distinct misconfigurations produce this symptom and are frequently confused:\\\\n\\\\n* **Wrong IAM action namespace.** The boto3 client ID for the Bedrock agent-runtime service\\\\n is `bedrock-agent-runtime`, but the IAM action namespace is `bedrock:`. A statement that\\\\n grants `bedrock-agent-runtime:Retrieve` or `bedrock-agent-runtime:RetrieveAndGenerate` is\\\\n syntactically valid IAM but grants nothing \u2014 these action strings do not exist in the IAM\\\\n service authorization tables. The correct actions are `bedrock:Retrieve` and\\\\n `bedrock:RetrieveAndGenerate`. A policy containing only the wrong-namespace actions will\\\\n produce an `implicitDeny` on simulation and an `AccessDeniedException` at runtime.\\\\n* **Missing cross-account Knowledge Base ID in the agent configuration.** If the agent\u2019s\\\\n `Config` object is populated from environment variables but the field for the Knowledge\\\\n Base identifier is not declared in the dataclass and not wired through the deployment\\\\n pipeline, `getattr(config, \\\\\"adp_kb_id\\\\\", \\\\\"\\\\\")` resolves to the empty string. Retrieve calls\\\\n issued against an empty KB ID silently fall back to local corpora rather than raising an\\\\n exception, making the misconfiguration invisible until grounding quality is inspected.\\\\n\\\\n**Resolution.**\\\\n\\\\n1. Audit every IAM policy statement on the AgentCore execution role that references Bedrock\\\\n Knowledge Base actions. Replace any `bedrock-agent-runtime:Retrieve` or\\\\n `bedrock-agent-runtime:RetrieveAndGenerate` action strings with `bedrock:Retrieve` and\\\\n `bedrock:RetrieveAndGenerate`. Redeploy the role policy and confirm with\\\\n `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` that the result changes from `implicitDeny`\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/guidance/latest/agentic-vehicle-experience-on-aws/ts-kb-access-denied.html\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be.
